desc:
A huge vector is mostly zeros, so it is stored sparsely as two parallel arrays: idx holds the positions of the stored entries in strictly increasing order, and val holds the entry at each of those positions. Every position that is not listed is zero.

Vector A is given by idxA and valA, vector B by idxB and valB. Return the dot product of the two vectors: the sum of A[p] * B[p] over all positions p.

idxA = [0, 3, 8, 20]   valA = [2, -1, 5, 4]
idxB = [3, 4, 8, 9]    valB = [6, 7, 2, 1]
result = (-1)*6 + 5*2 = 4

Only positions stored in both vectors contribute to the sum.
constraints: 0 ≤ idx[i] ≤ 10<sup>9</sup>, and each idx array is strictly increasing
hints: Building full-length dense vectors is impossible, positions go up to 10<sup>9</sup>. Work only with the stored entries.
A dictionary from position to value for one vector works. But both index arrays are sorted, so no dictionary is needed.
Use two pointers over the index arrays: when the indices are equal multiply the values and advance both; otherwise advance the pointer with the smaller index.
editorial: Only positions present in both vectors contribute, so the task is exactly the intersection of two sorted index lists. Keep a pointer into each list. If idxA[i] == idxB[j] add valA[i] * valB[j] to the answer and advance both. Otherwise the smaller index cannot occur in the other list any more, so advance that pointer.

Each step advances at least one pointer, giving O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space. With at most 5,000 entries of magnitude at most 100 the sum is at most 5,000 · 10,000 = 5 · 10<sup>7</sup>, comfortably inside 32 bits. When one vector is much shorter than the other, binary searching each of its indices in the longer one is an alternative.
